Chapter 22

The design system

Tokens with light-dark(), a theme class on MediaQuery, the boot script that stops the flash, fonts from fontsource preloaded by filename, an <enhanced:img> hero, one GSAP timeline as an attachment, motion tokens that reduced motion zeroes, and the short, named list of places a hex code may appear outside the tokens.

By the end of this chapter

Build a light-and-dark design system that never flashes, respects reduced motion, and keeps every colour in one file.

Four CSS files, imported in order: tokens define, reset clears, base styles, utilities lay out. Every colour, size and duration the interface uses is named once in the first, and components reference the names. A hex code anywhere else in src is a copy made where a custom property cannot be read, and there are four, each saying so where it is written: the map’s canvas (map/style.ts), the globe’s WebGL scene, the custom element’s shadow root, and the theme-color meta tags in app.html, which the browser reads before any stylesheet. The header of tokens.css lists them, along with the two hex codes that are not copies: print, which is black on white whatever the theme, and the #000 in a mask-image gradient, which means “opaque”, not black.

light-dark() is the whole theming mechanism. Each token holds its light value and its dark value and the browser picks by color-scheme, which follows the system by default and is pinned by data-theme on <html> when a person chooses. No duplicated @media (prefers-color-scheme) blocks, no .dark cascade, and — because the choice is applied before the first paint — no flash. The palette is “a map on a table, lit like a film”: warm paper in four surface tiers, ink in four weights, one teal that reads as water, and one hue per kind of stop that the itinerary and the map share through --kind-*. Three of the tokens exist only because of contrast arithmetic: --on-fill is the ink that reads on every kind colour in both themes (white fails on the pastel dark kinds at 1.9:1); the light --ink-3 was darkened until tertiary text passed 4.5:1 on every tier; and --segment-edge is the 1px edge a chosen segment draws — the theme toggle, the notes toolbar, the stop’s kind — because the tier step alone is 1.1:1 in dark and 1.2:1 in light, a state nobody can see, and the edge is 3:1 or better against both the track and the segment. The --night tokens are the one family that is not light-dark(): the globe is a night scene in both themes. The scale has eight steps, each a clamp() between a 360px phone and a 1280px desktop, with a leading and a tracking token to pair with each — big serif closes up, small serif is left alone — and most durations are a --dur-* that the prefers-reduced-motion block at the bottom sets to zero. Not all: the view transitions, the live dot’s pulse and the home page’s card stagger write their timing as numbers, and the tab indicator’s tween, the list’s flip and the map’s camera are JavaScript. Each of those sits behind a reduced-motion check of its own, and the comment above the block names every one — “reads a token” and “is switched off” are two different claims, and the second is the one that matters.

The display face is Fraunces, a variable font with an optical-size axis that the browser maps from the font size — font-optical-sizing: auto, so an 18px heading gets the cut drawn for 18px and a 56px hero gets the one drawn for posters; only the hero title and the 404 numeral pin "opsz" 144. The body is Inter. Both come from fontsource as stylesheets of @font-face rules with unicode-range, so a browser downloads the latin subset and nothing else — and chapter 14’s preload filter names those two files by their source filename.

The theme, and the flash it prevents

MediaQuery from svelte/reactivity is the system’s preference as a reactive value: when the operating system switches at sunset, resolved changes and the toaster and the map style follow, without anybody polling. The class only decides what color-scheme is; the CSS does the work. browser from $app/env guards the storage reads, because this module is imported on the server too.

The one inline script in the app, and the reason vite.config.ts hashes it. A dark choice on a light system would otherwise paint light for one frame before hydration; this runs before the first paint and sets data-theme from storage. It carries no nonce attribute, because the guides are prerendered and SvelteKit refuses to prerender a template with %sveltekit.nonce% in it — the hash in script-src allows it everywhere.

A radio group, because that is what it is: one of three, always exactly one. Arrow keys move between them for free, and a screen reader says “Theme, Light, 2 of 3” with no ARIA beyond the fieldset. :has(input:checked) styles the label from the state of the input inside it, which is what :has() was made for — and what it paints is a tier-3 pill with the --segment-edge hairline, so the choice shows in the dark theme too.

A picture that is four pictures

<enhanced:img> is rewritten at build time — by the preprocessor that must come first in vite.config.ts — into a <picture> with AVIF and WebP sources at several widths, plus width and height so nothing shifts while it loads. sizes tells the browser how wide the image is on screen, so it picks the smallest file that is still sharp. The source PNG is drawn by scripts/make-hero.ts with sharp, which is why sharp is a devDependency named out loud rather than a transitive one hoped for. It is drawn on cream, and on a dark page a cream print is the brightest thing on the screen; so in the dark theme the image is developed as a negative — filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg), a little darker and flatter — which turns the paper near-black and puts the teal route back to teal. On a phone a mask fades both its top and bottom edges into the page.

One timeline, three rules

The project’s cinematic budget is spent on the globe and on one hero. Everything else moves the way a good editor cuts: rarely, and for a reason — a dialog rises 8px, a bottom sheet slides on the iOS curve, a tab indicator is a Tween from svelte/motion, the check mark on a copy button pops in with a ten-line custom transition in src/lib/motion/transitions.ts, and all of it reads its duration from the --dur-* tokens or from the one MediaQuery in src/lib/motion/prefers.svelte.ts. The hero is the exception that earns GSAP: an attachment — a function that receives an element and returns a cleanup — with three rules the comment states: nothing is hidden until JavaScript runs, reduced motion means no motion, and it plays once. The copy and the image are found by data-hero-copy and data-hero-image, so the attachment does not know the markup, and the cleanup kills the timeline and clears the inline styles GSAP wrote. It is imported by the home route alone, so the library ships in that chunk and no other.

The feature cards need no timeline, so they get none. inview only decides *when*: it sets data-animate in the browser while the grid is still below the fold, and data-inview the first time it scrolls into view, and then disconnects its observer. The CSS does the motion — a 12px rise on --dur-5, each card 70ms after the one before through the --i the markup sets — and rule 1 lives in the selector: a card is hidden only under [data-animate], which the server never writes, so with JavaScript off every card is simply there. A grid already on screen when the script arrives skips the hiding step, and under reduced motion the whole block sits inside a media query that does not match.

Checkpoint

  • You can explain light-dark() and why the theme class only sets color-scheme.
  • You know why the boot script has a hash and no nonce.
  • You can state the three rules of the hero timeline, and say why the feature cards animate with CSS instead.
